output.title: Exit plans get expensive when the workflow stays in your head
output.body:
If you run a small business, the cost of an exit plan is often not the lawyer or the spreadsheet. It is the work that still lives in your head.

In the persona scenario Bareni uses, the owner is already spending roughly 8–10 hours a week on repeat customer questions, neglected leads, and manual invoice work. That is not a market statistic; it is just a useful picture of a common bottleneck. If that work stays manual, it is harder to write down the process, train someone else, or hand the business over cleanly later.

The bounded decision is simple: pick one recurring task and ask whether it is repeatable enough to automate before you think about anything bigger. Customer-inquiry triage, invoice logging, and lead routing are all examples of the kind of work that can be checked this way. If the answer is yes, the next step is a small diagnostic: define the workflow, the control point, and what “done” looks like.

That is the kind of scope Bareni looks at: one recurring workflow, one honest check on whether AI fits, then a one-page pilot proposal if it does. The timings are intended scopes, not guarantees. Final approval stays human, including any money movement or other high-risk decision.

Exit plans get cheaper when the routine work is no longer hiding inside the founder’s day. The first audit is usually unglamorous: which task ate the most time this week?
